questions.title: Zero values and safe APIs
questions.prompt: Is every zero value ready for every operation?
answerPoints: A declaration always initializes storage. Numeric values start at zero; pointers, maps, slices, channels and interfaces start nil. A struct recursively receives zero-valued fields.

Usable does not mean every operation succeeds: appending to a nil slice works, assigning a nil map panics, and sending to a nil channel blocks. A zero mutex is ready; a service needing configuration should say so in a constructor.
Design a type so its zero value is useful where reasonable. When setup is required, validate it at the boundary and document ownership instead of relying on hidden initialization.
questions.trap: “Everything is usable because Go has zero values” hides invalid operations on nil maps and channels.
questions.exercise: Compare appending to var s []int with assigning m["x"] = 1 after var m map[string]int.
questions.solution: append returns a valid slice containing the value. The map assignment panics until make or a map literal supplies a map. Test both the documented nil behavior and the ordinary path.
questions.followUp: How would your type distinguish an omitted limit from an explicitly configured zero?
questions.code:
var s []int
s = append(s, 1)
m := make(map[string]int)
m["x"] = 1

questions.title: Slice copies share storage
questions.prompt: Why did appending to one slice change another?
answerPoints: Assigning a slice copies its descriptor, not its backing array. Length controls indexing; capacity bounds reslicing and determines whether append can reuse storage.
If capacity permits, append writes into the shared array. Growing beyond capacity creates a new backing array, so code must use the returned slice. The growth factor is not a language contract.
Use copy or slices.Clone when independent storage is required. A full slice expression limits append capacity but still shares the existing elements; it is not a deep copy.
questions.trap: A capacity limit prevents append aliasing, but mutation of existing elements is still shared.
questions.exercise: Predict base after the code, then change left to base[:1:1].
questions.solution: Initially base becomes [1 9 3]. With capacity one, append allocates and base stays [1 2 3]. In both cases assigning left[0] before growth would mutate base[0].
questions.followUp: Explain which assumption would change your choice, and show a test that detects that change.
questions.complexity: Copying a slice descriptor: O(1). Cloning n elements: O(n) time and storage.

questions.title: Bytes, runes and text
questions.prompt: What does len(s) count, and when does range give the wrong index for a UI?
answerPoints: A Go string is an immutable sequence of bytes. len reports bytes; indexing yields a byte. UTF-8 is common but a string may contain arbitrary bytes.
range decodes UTF-8 and yields byte offsets plus runes. A rune is a Unicode code point, not necessarily a user-perceived character: combining sequences and emoji can contain multiple code points.

Choose semantics first: byte protocols use bytes, code-point operations use runes, and human text cursor movement needs grapheme-aware rules. Converting repeatedly to []rune allocates and loses the original byte-index relationship.
questions.trap: “Rune equals character” fails for combining marks and joined emoji.
questions.exercise: For "Go世", give byte length, rune count and the offsets produced by range.
questions.solution: The UTF-8 byte length is 5; there are 3 runes at byte offsets 0, 1 and 2. Use explicit UTF-8 fixtures and invalid-byte cases when testing parsers.
questions.followUp: How do you truncate untrusted UTF-8 without cutting a multi-byte encoding?

questions.title: Typed nil and method sets
questions.prompt: Why can err != nil even though its pointer is nil?
answerPoints: An interface value carries a dynamic type and value. A nil *Problem stored in error still supplies a dynamic type; only an interface with no dynamic type or value compares equal to nil.

T and *T have different method sets. A value with only pointer-receiver methods does not satisfy the corresponding interface even though an addressable variable may use an implicit address in a method call.
Return literal nil for the successful error result. Keep interfaces near their consumers and small enough to describe the needed behavior. Avoid interface{} just to make every implementation fit.
questions.trap: A successful method call on an addressable value does not prove that the value type satisfies an interface.
questions.exercise: Implement an error with a pointer receiver and return a typed nil; then fix the success path.
questions.solution: Returning (*Problem)(nil) as error creates a non-nil interface. A branch returning nil keeps the error interface nil. Add a test on the public error result, not on the internal pointer.
questions.followUp: When is a nil receiver method useful, and why must it check the receiver before dereferencing it?

questions.title: Errors are part of the API
questions.prompt: Should every error be wrapped, logged and retried?
answerPoints: Add context with fmt.Errorf and %w only when the cause is useful to callers; wrapping exposes matching behavior as part of the contract. errors.Is checks a target through the tree; errors.As extracts an assignable error type.
Classify at a boundary: invalid input, not found, conflict, cancellation and transient dependency failure need different responses. A transport timeout can leave a remote write outcome unknown.

Log once where ownership of handling ends, preserving request correlation and avoiding credentials. Retry only when the operation and budget allow it; wrapping or logging cannot make a non-idempotent action safe.
questions.trap: Matching error strings is brittle; retrying every timeout can duplicate side effects.
questions.exercise: A payment write times out after the server may have committed. What should the caller do?
questions.solution: Use an idempotency key or lookup by a stable operation ID to reconcile the outcome. Return a meaningful classification without inventing certainty. Test commit-then-disconnect, not just failure-before-write.
questions.followUp: How would joining multiple errors affect code that only calls Unwrap once?

questions.title: Generics, interfaces and typed code
questions.prompt: When should a reusable function be generic?
answerPoints: Use a type parameter when an algorithm has the same type-safe implementation for several types and preserving that type matters, such as a collection transform. Use a behavior interface when implementations differ behind operations.

Constraints define permitted operations. comparable allows equality but not ordering; ~int admits named types with underlying int. A type parameter does not supply arbitrary fields or dynamic methods.
Prefer a concrete function when only one case exists. Evaluate readability and generated code with real tooling instead of assuming generics remove all runtime costs or always cause boxing.
questions.trap: Replacing every interface with a type parameter often complicates APIs without preserving any useful relationship.
questions.exercise: Write a generic Contains function and explain why it cannot accept []map[string]int.
questions.solution: Contains[T comparable] can compare T with ==. Maps are not comparable except to nil; choose a key projection or equality function when semantic equality is needed.
questions.followUp: Explain which assumption would change your choice, and show a test that detects that change.
questions.complexity: O(n) comparisons; comparison cost depends on T.

questions.title: Defer arguments and return values
questions.prompt: When are deferred function arguments evaluated?
answerPoints: The function value and arguments of a deferred call are evaluated when the defer statement executes; the call itself runs when the surrounding function returns. Deferred calls run in last-in, first-out order.

A deferred closure can read variables at execution time, so defer fmt.Println(x) and defer func(){fmt.Println(x)}() need not print the same value. Named result variables can also be modified by a deferred closure after the return expression is assigned.

Use defer to make cleanup ownership clear, but do not accumulate thousands of open resources by deferring inside a long-running loop. Move one iteration into a function when each iteration should close its resource promptly.
questions.trap: A deferred call does not postpone evaluation of its already supplied arguments.
questions.exercise: x starts at1; defer fmt.Println(x); set x to2. What prints? What if the deferred code is a closure reading x?
questions.solution: The direct deferred call prints1 because its argument was captured at defer time. A closure reading x at return prints2. If both are deferred, the later defer runs first. Test resource close errors when they affect correctness instead of ignoring them reflexively.
questions.followUp: Why does deferring file.Close inside a huge file-processing loop keep too many descriptors open?
questions.code:
x := 1
defer fmt.Println(x)
defer func() { fmt.Println(x) }()
x = 2

questions.title: Panic, recover and failure boundaries
questions.prompt: Can a parent goroutine recover a child goroutine's panic?
answerPoints: recover only stops a panic when called directly by a deferred function on the panicking goroutine's stack. A parent goroutine's deferred recovery does not catch an unrelated child panic.

Use errors for expected failures such as invalid input or unavailable storage. Panic usually represents a violated invariant or programming error; recovery at a server boundary can protect the process but cannot prove shared state remains valid.
Cleanup still needs ownership and error reporting. Do not convert every panic into a successful zero result, and do not use panic/recover as ordinary cross-goroutine control flow.
questions.trap: A defer in main is not a global panic handler for every goroutine.
questions.exercise: A worker panics after updating half a shared structure. Is recovering and retrying automatically safe?
questions.solution: No. Recovery prevents stack unwinding from ending the process only within its valid boundary; it does not roll back partial mutations. Restore or discard inconsistent state according to the invariant, and report the failure. Prefer atomic state transitions and test the failure boundary.
questions.followUp: Which errors should an HTTP recovery middleware hide from a public response while retaining diagnostic evidence?

questions.title: Map order, nil maps and concurrency
questions.prompt: Can you rely on iteration order or read a map during a concurrent write?
answerPoints: Map iteration order is unspecified. Tests or output requiring stable order must sort keys or use an explicitly ordered representation. A nil map can be read and has length zero, but assignment requires an initialized map.

Ordinary maps do not support unsynchronized concurrent read/write access. Protect the whole invariant with a lock, publish immutable snapshots, or choose a specialized concurrent structure for a measured use case.

A map lookup can return a zero value for either a missing key or a present zero. Use the comma-ok result when that distinction matters. Deleting a key does not promise immediate shrinking of all backing memory.
questions.trap: Several readers are safe only while no goroutine writes without the required synchronization.
questions.exercise: A map[string]int contains a real score0. How do you distinguish it from an absent user?
questions.solution: Use value, ok := scores[id]. The value0 alone is ambiguous. For deterministic output, copy keys and sort them; do not infer insertion order from a few test runs.
questions.followUp: Why can sync.Map be a poor replacement for several map operations that must be atomic together?

questions.title: Everything is passed by value
questions.prompt: If Go passes by value, why can a function modify a caller's slice elements?
answerPoints: Function arguments are copied values. Copying a slice copies a descriptor referring to the same backing storage; copying a pointer copies an address, and copying a map value still refers to the same map data.

Reassigning the local slice variable changes only that local descriptor. Mutating an existing element can be visible to the caller. Appending may allocate, so return the updated slice rather than assume the caller's length changes.

Copying a struct copies its fields, not a recursively independent object graph. A struct containing a slice or pointer can still share mutable data. Do not copy synchronization values such as an already-used mutex.
questions.trap: “Slices are passed by reference” hides the copied descriptor and leads to wrong expectations about append.
questions.exercise: A function appends to its []int argument but does not return it. Does the caller's length change?
questions.solution: No. The function changed its local slice descriptor. Writes into shared backing capacity may still affect other views, which is precisely why returning the descriptor and defining ownership matters.
questions.followUp: How would you design an API that promises it will not retain or mutate a caller's buffer?

questions.title: Loop variables and toolchain semantics
questions.prompt: Do all goroutines in a range loop still capture the same iteration variable?
answerPoints: It depends on how the variable is declared and on the language version used by the module. Modern Go changed semantics for loop-declared iteration variables; repeating the old universal capture warning is inaccurate.

A variable declared outside the loop and assigned by the loop can still be shared across iterations. Shared pointed-to objects and other mutable fixtures also remain shared even when each iteration variable is distinct.

Inspect the go directive and actual declaration, then write explicit ownership where it improves clarity. Passing a value as a goroutine argument can make the captured value obvious, but does not deep-copy referenced data or provide a join.
questions.trap: New loop semantics do not make every loop-spawned goroutine race-free or bounded.
questions.exercise: Compare for _, v := range xs with var v T; for _, v = range xs when closures retain v.
questions.solution: In modules using the new language semantics, the first form declares per-iteration variables; the second assigns the same existing variable. For both forms, pointed-to data can still be shared and goroutines must still be joined.
questions.followUp: Why does a parallel table test still fail if every case mutates the same fake server?

questions.title: Comparability and map keys
questions.prompt: Why can using any as a map key panic?
answerPoints: Map keys require a comparable key type. Arrays and structs are comparable only when their components are; slices, maps and functions are not generally comparable except their permitted nil comparisons.

An interface value is comparable when its dynamic value is comparable. A map[any]int can therefore compile but panic when used with a slice as the dynamic key. A generic comparable constraint has its own language rules; do not assume it validates arbitrary dynamic data recursively.
Choose stable, explicit key types. If semantic equality involves slices or normalized text, define canonicalization or hashing with collision handling and preserve the original equality contract.
questions.trap: The static type any does not make every dynamic key valid for hashing or equality.
questions.exercise: What happens with keys[[]int{1,2}] = 3 in a map[any]int?
questions.solution: It panics because the interface contains an unhashable slice. Use a comparable domain key, such as a fixed array where appropriate, or an explicitly encoded canonical key with documented semantics.
questions.followUp: What happens when a struct key contains a float64 NaN?

questions.title: io.Reader: data and an error together
questions.prompt: Should a read loop discard bytes when Read returns an error?
answerPoints: Read can return n>0 together with an error, including EOF. Process the n bytes before handling the error, or a final partial chunk may be lost. A short read alone is not necessarily EOF.
Use io.ReadFull when an exact fixed-size record is required and inspect its documented errors. Use streaming decoders for structured input, enforce limits and preserve incomplete-record behavior.

A buffer may be reused on the next call. Copy retained bytes or transfer ownership explicitly before handing them to an asynchronous consumer; otherwise the next read can overwrite data still being used.
questions.trap: A loop that checks err first can silently drop the final bytes of a valid stream.
questions.exercise: A reader returns n3 and io.EOF on the same call. What must the consumer do?
questions.solution: Consume the first3 bytes, then handle EOF as end of input. If a protocol required4 bytes, treat that as a truncated record according to the protocol. Test n>0+EOF explicitly with a custom reader.
questions.followUp: Why is io.Copy often safer than inventing an ad hoc copy loop?

questions.title: Integer width, overflow and representation
questions.prompt: Does int always have64 bits, and do integer operations panic on overflow?
answerPoints: int width is implementation-dependent within the language's specified choices; use an explicit-width type when a wire format or persistence contract requires one. Parsing must check range and errors.

Integer overflow behavior is defined by Go's integer rules and does not generally panic like a bounds check. A sum, size multiplication or length conversion can overflow before an allocation or validation step.

Validate untrusted sizes before arithmetic using bounds that avoid performing the overflowing operation. Signed/unsigned conversions can change meaning, so do not cast a negative length to uint and expect it to become safe.
questions.trap: Switching every size to uint does not remove overflow and can turn negative input into a huge positive number.
questions.exercise: How do you check count × elementSize against a memory budget without overflowing the product?
questions.solution: After validating nonnegative count and positive elementSize, compare count to budget/elementSize before multiplying. Then validate target int/address-space constraints. Test the exact boundary, one over and negative parsed input.
questions.followUp: Where does an unchecked distance addition break an otherwise correct shortest-path algorithm?

questions.title: Stack, heap and escape analysis
questions.prompt: Does returning a pointer always allocate on the heap?
answerPoints: The compiler decides placement from escape analysis and other constraints; source syntax alone does not determine the final allocation. Returning an address is safe because the compiler keeps storage alive as needed.

Inlining and calling context can change escape decisions. Large objects or values passed into opaque interfaces may allocate even when their source appears local. Compiler diagnostics are evidence for a particular build.

Measure allocations with representative benchmarks and inspect go build -gcflags=-m=2 output. Optimize a hot path only after identifying it; do not turn every value into a pointer or introduce unsafe to chase a guess.
questions.trap: “Pointers always live on the heap” confuses the pointer value with the object it points to.
questions.exercise: Compare allocations for returning a small struct value and returning its address, with and without inlining.
questions.solution: Benchmark both observable call paths and avoid a discarded-result benchmark that the compiler can eliminate. Use benchmem and compiler output together; do not promise an invariant allocation count across compiler versions.
questions.followUp: What can change when the same function is called through an interface?

questions.title: GC budgets under load
questions.prompt: Why can a service with little live data still spend substantial CPU in GC?
answerPoints: Allocation rate drives how quickly another collection is needed; the collector must scan reachable objects, not just count the final heap size. Short-lived allocations can create significant work even with a modest live heap.
GOGC trades collection frequency against heap growth. GOMEMLIMIT is a soft runtime memory limit, not a hard cap on total process or container RSS; non-Go memory and runtime overhead still matter.

Measure allocation profiles, live heap, GC CPU and tail latency under a representative request rate. Reduce needless allocation or pointer-rich retention before tuning, and leave headroom below the container limit.
questions.trap: Setting GOMEMLIMIT equal to the container cap leaves no budget for other process memory.
questions.exercise: After reducing the memory limit, CPU increases and p99 worsens. Explain the feedback loop.
questions.solution: A tighter heap budget can trigger more GC work, leaving less CPU to finish requests; queued requests retain more memory. Bound admission, inspect GC metrics and retune with headroom rather than only increasing goroutines.
questions.followUp: Which profile distinguishes allocation churn from a long-lived retention leak?

questions.title: Retention, pools and ownership
questions.prompt: Can a tiny slice retain a very large allocation?
answerPoints: A slice keeps its backing array reachable. Keeping a short subslice of a large buffer can retain the full allocation; retaining pointer elements may also retain their referenced objects.

Copy only the needed bytes into independent storage when lifetime separation matters. Clearing obsolete pointers helps release referenced objects, but it does not shrink the backing allocation itself.

sync.Pool is a temporary allocation reuse mechanism whose contents may disappear at any time. Do not use it as a durable cache, a resource limit, or a place to return buffers still referenced by a response.
questions.trap: Returning a buffer to a pool while another goroutine still reads it creates corruption or a data race.
questions.exercise: A parser stores the first 20 bytes of each 20 MB request. How would you test and fix retention?
questions.solution: Copy the retained token into a small independent allocation, release the request and compare live heap after collection in a controlled test. Keep the measurement separate from a throughput benchmark.
questions.followUp: How would oversized pooled buffers change memory use after a rare large request?

questions.title: Goroutines, threads and CPU quotas
questions.prompt: Why does adding goroutines fail to speed up CPU work?
answerPoints: Goroutines are scheduled by the runtime onto OS threads. GOMAXPROCS limits simultaneous execution of Go code; it is not a limit on goroutine count or every OS thread.

CPU-bound work only benefits until CPU capacity and parallelizable work are exhausted. More runnable goroutines can add scheduling overhead, cache misses and memory pressure. Blocking I/O has different behavior.
Account for the runtime version and container CPU policy when inspecting the effective GOMAXPROCS. Use CPU profiles, runtime traces and cgroup throttling metrics before choosing worker counts.
questions.trap: One goroutine per task with an unbounded queue is not a CPU capacity strategy.
questions.exercise: A two-CPU container starts 1,000 hashing workers and p99 grows. What do you change first?
questions.solution: Bound active hashing workers and queue length, measure throughput and CPU throttling, then compare a small range of concurrency limits. Reject or defer overload instead of retaining unlimited work.
questions.followUp: How does blocking in a syscall differ from spending all CPU time in Go code?

questions.title: Memory layout and false sharing
questions.prompt: Two independent counters slow down when updated concurrently. Why?
answerPoints: CPU caches move cache lines, so different variables sharing a line may still contend when different cores write them. This is false sharing; there need not be a language-level data race.

An atomic counter can be race-free and still expensive under contention. Sharding, per-worker aggregation or batching can reduce cache coherence traffic, while padding trades memory for potential isolation.

Demonstrate the bottleneck with a realistic benchmark and profiles on target hardware. Do not hardcode a universal cache-line size or rearrange every struct on speculation. Preserve synchronization correctness while measuring layout changes.
questions.trap: The absence of race detector warnings says nothing about cache-line contention.
questions.exercise: Design a throughput metric for 64 workers that does not require one global atomic on every item.
questions.solution: Use per-worker counts and aggregate after joining, or periodically batch increments if live estimates are needed. Explain how often a reader needs fresh data and how that choice changes synchronization.
questions.followUp: Why can a mutex outperform a spin-based retry loop under heavy contention?

questions.title: When unsafe and cgo change the contract
questions.prompt: Can you keep a C pointer to Go memory after a cgo call?
answerPoints: Go and C have distinct lifetime and pointer rules. Whether a pointer may cross a call depends on what memory contains, how long it is retained and whether pinning is permitted and managed. Consult the current cgo rules rather than treating a pointer cast as authorization.

C allocations are not reclaimed by Go GC. Allocate/free ownership must be explicit, errors must release partial resources and callbacks must obey lifetime restrictions. A Go finalizer is not a timely cleanup protocol.
Prefer copying a bounded buffer or an established wrapper when possible. Account for foreign allocations in process memory and deploy the required libc/native libraries for the chosen target.
questions.trap: unsafe.Pointer changes the type system view; it does not extend lifetime or legalize retained pointers.
questions.exercise: A wrapper leaks memory but the Go heap profile stays flat. Where do you investigate?
questions.solution: Measure RSS and native allocations, audit every C allocation/free pair and error path, and check retained handles and callback lifetimes. Go heap profiles cannot attribute every byte allocated by foreign libraries.
questions.followUp: Why can enabling cgo change cross-compilation and the suitability of a scratch container?

questions.title: Channel closure is a protocol
questions.prompt: Who closes a channel used by several workers?
answerPoints: Closing announces that no more values will be sent; it is not mandatory garbage-collection cleanup. Sending on a closed channel panics; receivers can drain buffered values and then observe ok == false.

The owner that can prove all senders have finished closes once. With several producers, a coordinator waits for them before closing the results channel. A consumer cancels upstream work through a separate context or signal.
A nil channel disables a select case but blocks outside select. Reading from a closed channel succeeds immediately, so a loop must exit or disable that case instead of spinning.
questions.trap: A receiver closing the results channel because it has enough values can race with a still-active sender.
questions.exercise: Design the ordering for three producers and one collector that can stop early.
questions.solution: Give producers a cancellation context, make sends selectable on cancellation, join all producers and close results from one coordinator. The collector may stop after cancellation, but senders must still be able to finish.
questions.followUp: How does the result change for a buffered channel that is closed while values remain?

questions.title: Cancellation is not joining
questions.prompt: Does calling cancel guarantee a goroutine has stopped?
answerPoints: A context signals cancellation and carries deadlines; it does not forcibly terminate goroutines. A function must observe it and propagate it into context-aware I/O.
Join workers explicitly with a WaitGroup, errgroup or a completion channel. Code still needs cleanup after cancellation, and its cleanup must have a bounded, appropriate context.
Make every potentially blocking point cancellable, including acquiring capacity and sending results. A context value should hold request-scoped metadata, not become a dependency container.
questions.trap: Launching a goroutine to abandon an uncancellable operation can merely move the leak.
questions.exercise: A producer blocks at out <- result after the caller returns. Repair that send.
questions.solution: Select between sending the result and ctx.Done. Ensure the receiver also joins workers and that the underlying work observes cancellation. A select is not a promise of strict priority if both cases are ready.
questions.followUp: Why should cleanup sometimes use a new bounded context instead of an already-cancelled request context?

questions.title: Data races versus business races
questions.prompt: Why is a check-then-insert still wrong with a mutex around each operation?
answerPoints: A data race is concurrent unsynchronized conflicting access to memory. A logical race can occur even when each individual access is synchronized, if a multi-step invariant is not atomic.

Protect the entire read-check-write operation under one lock, use a database conditional write/unique constraint, or transfer ownership to one goroutine. Choose the scope where the invariant actually lives.
The race detector observes executed memory accesses. It can reveal data races on covered paths but cannot prove every interleaving safe or detect every distributed lost update.
questions.trap: “The map methods lock internally, so the sequence is safe” misses the gap between methods.
questions.exercise: Two requests each see no username and both create it. What is the final authority?
questions.solution: A uniqueness constraint in the authoritative store must decide. A process-local mutex cannot coordinate several replicas, and a precheck can only improve the user experience, not enforce uniqueness.
questions.followUp: Which deterministic concurrency test would demonstrate the gap using a barrier?

questions.title: Happens-before, not wishful timing
questions.prompt: Can another goroutine safely read a value after sleeping?
answerPoints: Time passing does not create a synchronization relationship. A send/receive, mutex unlock/lock or documented atomic operation can establish ordering; a sleep cannot.
The Go memory model defines the guarantees for correctly synchronized programs. Publishing a pointer before fully initializing the object can expose unsafe state without proper synchronization.

Use the smallest synchronization protocol that also documents ownership. An atomic flag only helps when the associated access obeys the memory model; replacing one field with an atomic does not automatically protect the whole object.
questions.trap: A program that appears correct on your laptop can still contain a data race.
questions.exercise: Publish a configuration snapshot to readers without mutating the published snapshot.
questions.solution: Fully construct an immutable snapshot, then publish it through a mutex or an atomic pointer/value with a consistent stored type. Replace with a new snapshot on updates. Never mutate an already published map concurrently.
questions.followUp: How do you handle a snapshot that contains mutable slices or nested maps?

questions.title: Bounded workers and overload
questions.prompt: How do you keep one million jobs from becoming one million goroutines?
answerPoints: Separate queue capacity from worker count. A bounded queue caps retained waiting work; a worker limit caps active work. Each job still needs a deadline and a memory budget.

Define overload behavior: block with cancellation, reject, shed lower-priority jobs or persist work for later. A semaphore acquired inside a newly launched goroutine still permits unbounded waiting goroutines.
Own shutdown: stop intake, cancel or drain accepted work, wait for workers, then close resources. A results queue must also be bounded and cannot prevent workers from exiting.
questions.trap: A large channel buffer postpones overload while increasing latency and retained memory.
questions.exercise: An endpoint accepts 10,000 jobs/second but capacity is 1,000. Which metric reveals the problem before a crash?
questions.solution: Queue age and length expose the mismatch; rejection count and end-to-end latency show the chosen policy. Add admission control at intake, then measure sustainable throughput under a fixed resource budget.
questions.followUp: What happens to fairness when a single tenant fills the shared queue?

questions.title: Select, timers and fairness
questions.prompt: Does select always prefer cancellation over a ready result?
answerPoints: When multiple cases can proceed, select chooses one pseudo-randomly. Source order does not prioritize cancellation. A default case makes the select nonblocking and can create a hot spin loop.

Deadlines require timers or context, not repeated sleep polling. Timer channel behavior changed in recent Go versions, so check the target toolchain and package contract instead of repeating an obsolete stop/drain recipe.
Specify acceptable semantics when cancellation and a result become ready together. If an API must never commit after cancellation, a select alone cannot provide a distributed transaction boundary.
questions.trap: Adding ctx.Done as the first case does not turn it into a strict priority queue.
questions.exercise: A worker sees both ctx.Done and a buffered job ready. Can it take the job?
questions.solution: Yes. Guard expensive work with an additional cancellation check if avoiding unnecessary work matters, but describe remaining races honestly. Enforce irreversible operation semantics in the authoritative protocol.
questions.followUp: Why can a select with a default case consume a full CPU while doing no useful work?

questions.title: Concurrent cache and stampedes
questions.prompt: How do you avoid 1,000 identical cache misses triggering 1,000 database reads?
answerPoints: A map lock protects map consistency but does not collapse identical loads. Use keyed in-flight work so callers for one key can share a result, with explicit error and cancellation behavior.
Avoid holding a global mutex across network I/O. Bound concurrent loads across distinct keys as well, because duplicate suppression alone does not limit a high-cardinality miss storm.

Define expiration jitter, negative-cache policy, stale serving and invalidation. A cache key must include the tenant and all query dimensions that affect the result. Instrument hit rate, load latency and origin demand.
questions.trap: Singleflight on one key does not solve many distinct misses or cross-replica stampedes.
questions.exercise: One caller cancels while nine still await the same key. Should it cancel the shared load?
questions.solution: Not automatically. Separate each waiter’s cancellation from a bounded shared load lifetime, and decide how to stop work after all waiters leave. Document whether stale data is acceptable during a refresh.
questions.followUp: How would you prevent a slow old refresh from overwriting a newer cached value?

questions.title: Deadlock and lock ordering
questions.prompt: How do you debug a service that is alive but no longer processes requests?
answerPoints: Capture goroutine stacks and look for common waits: a mutex held across I/O, a full channel with no consumer, a WaitGroup whose owner waits before starting the receiver, or a cyclic lock acquisition.
Use a consistent global lock order when two locks are unavoidable. Shrink critical sections and avoid callbacks under locks because callbacks can reenter code or acquire locks in unknown order.
A partial deadlock may not trigger the runtime all-goroutines-asleep panic while timers or background goroutines continue. Expose queue progress and dependency health, not just process liveness.
questions.trap: A running health endpoint does not prove the worker pipeline is making progress.
questions.exercise: A producer must finish before the main goroutine begins receiving an unbuffered results channel. Explain the cycle.
questions.solution: The producer cannot finish until a receiver accepts its send, while the receiver waits for producer completion. Receive concurrently, or arrange a coordinator to close after producers finish while the collector drains.
questions.followUp: What would a block profile add beyond one snapshot of goroutine stacks?

questions.title: Binary search as a boundary invariant
questions.prompt: Find the first index whose value is at least a target.
answerPoints: Maintain a half-open search interval [lo, hi). All indexes before lo are known too small; every candidate answer remains inside the interval or at n. The sorted-input precondition is essential.
Choose mid = lo + (hi-lo)/2. If xs[mid] < target, discard through mid; otherwise keep mid as a possible first answer by moving hi to mid. Each iteration strictly shrinks the interval.
Returning lo handles duplicates and missing targets uniformly; lo == len(xs) means no qualifying element. Test empty input, all equal values, target outside the range and an exact duplicate boundary.
questions.trap: Returning immediately on equality finds an arbitrary occurrence, not necessarily the first.
questions.exercise: For [1, 3, 3, 8] and target 3, trace every lo, hi and mid.
questions.solution: Start [0,4), mid2 qualifies → hi2. Mid1 qualifies → hi1. Mid0 is too small → lo1. Return1. For target9, return4. Use sort.Search or slices.BinarySearch when their contract matches.
questions.followUp: How would you find the last equal element without scanning all duplicates?
questions.complexity: O(log n) comparisons, O(1) extra storage. Useful for sorted event offsets and range boundaries.

questions.title: Two sum and index ownership
questions.prompt: Find two distinct indexes whose values sum to a target.
answerPoints: Scan once and map each previously seen value to an index. Before storing the current value, look for target-current; that ordering prevents using the current index twice.

Store and return indexes, not just values, because duplicates can form the answer. For [3,3] and target6, the second element finds the first. Define behavior when no pair exists or several pairs qualify.

Hash lookup gives expected constant time, not a universal worst-case guarantee. Bound input and consider integer overflow before computing the complement when values are untrusted or use the full int range.
questions.trap: Inserting the current element before lookup may return the same index twice.
questions.exercise: Trace [2,7,11,15] with target9 and then [3,3] with target6.
questions.solution: The first case stores2→0, then7 finds2 and returns(0,1). The second stores the first3, and the second3 finds index0. Test no result and duplicate values independently.
questions.followUp: If the input is sorted, when would two pointers be preferable to a map?
questions.complexity: Expected O(n) time and O(n) storage, assuming complement arithmetic fits int.

questions.title: Sliding window without repeated scans
questions.prompt: Find the longest byte substring with no repeated byte.
answerPoints: Maintain a window [left,right] containing unique bytes and a map of last positions. On a repeated byte, move left to max(left,last+1); never move left backward.
Each index enters and leaves the logical window at most once, so repeated characters do not require rescanning the window. Keep the best length and its start if the substring itself is needed.

The unit matters. This version operates on bytes and suits ASCII keys or byte protocols. A rune version needs rune positions or carefully tracked byte offsets; grapheme-aware text needs a different contract.
questions.trap: Assigning left = last+1 without max breaks on abba by moving the boundary backward.
questions.exercise: Trace "abba" and explain why the answer is2, then define what changes for emoji.
questions.solution: At the second b, left becomes2. The final a was last seen at0, outside the current window, so left stays2 and best remains2. For Unicode, first state whether uniqueness means code points or grapheme clusters.
questions.followUp: What changes for a longest window that contains at most k distinct values?
questions.complexity: O(n) time, O(min(n,256)) storage for bytes. Useful for bounded stream/window reasoning.

questions.title: BFS and shortest unweighted paths
questions.prompt: How do you find the fewest edges between two nodes?
answerPoints: Use a FIFO queue and mark a node visited when enqueuing it, not after dequeue. This prevents many parents from enqueueing the same node repeatedly. Set each newly discovered distance to parent distance+1.

BFS explores by increasing edge count, so the first discovery gives a shortest path in an unweighted graph. Store predecessor links to reconstruct the path; distance alone does not describe the route.

Disconnected nodes remain unreachable. A directed graph only permits listed outgoing edges. In Go, a head index avoids repeatedly shifting the queue; clear references or release the queue when retaining a long-lived backing array matters.
questions.trap: BFS is not a shortest-cost algorithm when edges have different weights.
questions.exercise: For A→B,C; B→D; C→D,E, find distance and one path from A to E.
questions.solution: Enqueue A, then B and C at distance1. B discovers D at2; C skips already discovered D and discovers E at2. Predecessors reconstruct A,C,E. Test a cycle and an unreachable node.
questions.followUp: How would a multi-source BFS model the nearest replica or facility?
questions.complexity: O(V+E) time and O(V) extra storage. Useful for dependency reachability and shortest hop count.

questions.title: Dijkstra and stale heap entries
questions.prompt: How do you find cheapest routes with nonnegative edge weights?
answerPoints: Keep the best known distance to every node and use a min-heap of candidate distances. Pop the smallest candidate, skip it if its distance is stale, and relax outgoing edges.

With nonnegative weights, a current minimum cannot later be improved through a more expensive unsettled path. Negative edges invalidate that argument; choose an appropriate algorithm rather than quietly accepting them.

A simple Go implementation can push a new entry for each improvement instead of decrease-key. Stale entries use more heap space but simplify ownership. Guard distance addition against overflow and define unreachable results explicitly.
questions.trap: Marking visited when enqueuing is correct for BFS, but can discard a later cheaper route in Dijkstra.
questions.exercise: A→B costs4, A→C costs1, C→B costs2. Which B entry becomes stale?
questions.solution: The heap first receives B4 and C1. Expanding C improves B to3; B3 is processed, and the later B4 entry is skipped. Returning as soon as B4 is inserted would produce the wrong route.
questions.followUp: Why does adding a heuristic require an admissibility/consistency argument in A*?
questions.complexity: With duplicate heap entries: O((V+E) log(V+E)) time and O(V+E) storage; tighter bounds depend on the heap strategy.

questions.title: Top-K with a bounded min-heap
questions.prompt: How can a stream keep its largest k values without sorting everything?
answerPoints: Keep a min-heap of at most k values. Its root is the smallest retained winner; once full, discard an incoming value no larger than the root, otherwise replace the root and restore the heap.

The invariant is that after each prefix the heap contains its k largest values, or every value if fewer than k arrived. Duplicates count separately unless the problem explicitly asks for distinct values.

Validate k, avoid retaining the full stream and sort only the final winners if ordered output is needed. container/heap expects you to implement its interface; its Push/Pop methods have different roles from calling heap.Push/heap.Pop.
questions.trap: A max-heap of k values exposes the largest winner, which is the wrong item to evict.
questions.exercise: Trace [5,1,9,3,8] with k3. Which items survive?
questions.solution: Fill with5,1,9. Replace root1 with3, then root3 with8. Winners are5,8,9; heap internal order is not sorted order. Test k0, k>n and duplicate cutoffs.
questions.followUp: How would you merge top-K results from several partitions without collecting every original value?
questions.complexity: O(n log k) time and O(k) storage, plus O(k log k) if final sorted output is requested.

questions.title: Merge sorted streams
questions.prompt: How do you merge two sorted inputs without re-sorting them?
answerPoints: Track the next unread element of each input. Emit the smaller and advance only its pointer, preserving the invariant that the output prefix is sorted and contains exactly the consumed elements.

When one input is exhausted, append or stream the remainder. Decide tie ordering: choosing the left element first preserves stability across the two sources. Never assume both inputs have equal length.

For k streams, keep one head per nonempty stream in a min-heap. For remote streams, also bound buffering and close every iterator on cancellation; algorithmic complexity does not describe network lifetime.
questions.trap: Concatenate-and-sort adds unnecessary work and cannot naturally stream an unbounded input.
questions.exercise: Merge [1,4,8] and [2,4,7], retaining left-before-right ties.
questions.solution: Emit1,2,4(left),4(right),7,8. Test one empty source and all-equal values. If the caller needs source stability, include source identity in the tie rule.
questions.followUp: What would you do if an input violates its promised sorted order halfway through?
questions.complexity: Two inputs: O(n+m) time, O(n+m) output. k streams: O(N log k) time with O(k) heap state.

questions.title: Dynamic programming: minimum coins
questions.prompt: Why does choosing the largest coin first fail for arbitrary denominations?
answerPoints: Greedy choice needs a proof for the denomination system. With coins1,3,4 and amount6, greedy gives4+1+1 while3+3 uses fewer coins. Dynamic programming reuses optimal answers for smaller amounts.
Define dp[0]=0 and dp[x] as the minimum coins for x. For each positive coin c≤x, consider dp[x-c]+1 if that state is reachable. Initialize other states to an unreachable sentinel.

Reject nonpositive denominations and bound the amount before allocation. Reconstruct chosen coins with a predecessor array if needed. For huge amounts or different constraints, this pseudo-polynomial method may be unsuitable.
questions.trap: A polynomial function of amount is not polynomial in the number of bits used to encode amount.
questions.exercise: Compute dp[0..6] for coins1,3,4, then explain an unreachable case with coins2,4 and amount3.
questions.solution: The first table is0,1,2,1,1,2,2. With only2 and4, odd amounts remain unreachable, so return an explicit no-solution result. Test amount0, duplicates, invalid coins and a memory budget limit.
questions.followUp: How does changing the loop order alter a count-the-combinations problem?
questions.complexity: O(amount × coinCount) time and O(amount) storage; pseudo-polynomial.

questions.title: Why Go for backend systems?
questions.prompt: Why choose Go for a network service, and when would you choose something else?
answerPoints: Go combines a compiled toolchain, goroutines, a substantial network standard library and explicit error handling. These make services, command-line tools and infrastructure agents practical to build and operate with relatively small language surface area.

This is a fit argument, not a claim that Go uniquely solves algorithms or is always fastest. GC, binary size, cgo dependencies, library maturity and team expertise affect the choice. Hard real-time work and specialized numerical kernels can require different tools.

Start with workload and constraints: latency budget, memory, deployment targets, concurrency model and integration needs. Compare a representative prototype with operational costs, not a microbenchmark of one loop.
questions.trap: “Go is concurrent, so every Go program is fast” ignores blocking, contention, allocation and algorithmic complexity.
questions.exercise: Choose between a Go API, a GPU training kernel and a tiny hard real-time interrupt handler.
questions.solution: Go is a plausible API choice with bounded concurrency and measured GC behavior. Use established GPU tooling for training kernels and a platform-appropriate real-time approach for strict interrupt deadlines. The best architecture may combine languages behind a narrow boundary.
questions.followUp: Which measurements would convince you that the initial language choice was wrong?

questions.title: Package boundaries and clean code
questions.prompt: What makes a Go package a useful boundary rather than an extra folder?
answerPoints: A package owns a cohesive responsibility and exposes a small contract. Name it for its domain or capability, not a vague layer such as utils. Keep dependency direction acyclic and hide implementation details with unexported identifiers and internal where appropriate.

Place small interfaces where behavior is consumed. Concrete types are often sufficient until there are actual alternate implementations or testing boundaries. Constructor parameters should make resource and configuration dependencies visible.

Clean code reduces the reader's work: meaningful names, short error paths, explicit ownership and focused tests. A uniform line count or one interface per struct is not a substitute for a clear invariant.
questions.trap: Moving every type into its own package increases navigation and can create artificial dependency cycles.
questions.exercise: Split a handler that validates input, charges a card and writes an order. Where is the transaction policy?
questions.solution: Keep HTTP decoding at the edge and payment/order orchestration in an application operation. Let storage expose the needed atomic operation. Do not pretend a database transaction can atomically include an arbitrary remote payment call; model retries and reconciliation.
questions.followUp: How would you avoid making your domain depend on a database driver type?

questions.title: Layered, hexagonal, vertical or services?
questions.prompt: How would you choose an architecture for a growing Go product?
answerPoints: Begin with deployment and team constraints. A modular monolith keeps transactions and operational work simple; vertical slices group a feature's changes; layered or hexagonal boundaries can isolate business decisions from transports and storage.

Microservices buy independent deployment and failure isolation only when boundaries and operations support them. They add network failures, compatibility, observability and data consistency work. CQRS separates read/write models; event sourcing retains events as the authority and introduces evolution/replay obligations.

Rate suitability against a concrete scenario rather than declare a universal winner. For a small CRUD service, a simple modular design may rate higher than event sourcing. For audit-heavy workflows, the replay cost may be justified. Record the tradeoff and revisit it as evidence changes.
questions.trap: Naming folders domain/application/infrastructure does not by itself create a clean dependency boundary.
questions.exercise: Two developers need an admin CRUD API next month. Rank simple modular monolith, microservices and event sourcing.
questions.solution: Usually start with the modular monolith: fewer deployments and local transactional invariants. Score the other options lower unless independent team ownership or immutable event history is a real requirement. This is a scenario-specific judgment, not a language-wide ranking.
questions.followUp: What observable change would justify extracting the first service?

questions.title: Patterns with a cost
questions.prompt: Which design patterns translate naturally into Go?
answerPoints: Composition, small interfaces and functions often implement strategy, adapter and decorator without an inheritance hierarchy. A function can express a policy; an io.Reader wrapper can add counting or limits around another reader.

Functional options can manage optional constructor settings, but required dependencies should remain obvious. A singleton that silently owns a database client hides lifetime and makes parallel tests harder; explicit construction is often clearer.

Use a pattern to solve an identified pressure. Explain the extra indirection, configuration ordering and error behavior. Prefer a direct implementation until two variations or a meaningful boundary justify abstraction.
questions.trap: Every pattern having a textbook class diagram does not mean the Go implementation needs the same classes.
questions.exercise: Add metrics around an existing Store without changing every caller or leaking credentials.
questions.solution: Wrap the consumed Store interface, time each operation, classify low-cardinality outcomes and forward context/results unchanged. Decide which layer owns retries and logs to avoid duplicate accounting.
questions.followUp: When does a decorator change semantics, for example by adding retries to a write?

questions.title: Idempotency, outbox and retries
questions.prompt: How do you keep an accepted order and its published event consistent?
answerPoints: A database commit and a remote broker publish are separate failure boundaries. Publishing before commit may announce rolled-back data; publishing after commit may be skipped if the process crashes.
Write an outbox record in the same transaction as the domain state. A relay publishes pending records and tracks progress. Crashing after publish but before marking sent can still duplicate delivery.

Consumers need a durable idempotency decision in the same atomic boundary as their side effect, using event/operation IDs. “Exactly once” must name the scope and failure model; an in-memory dedup set is not durable correctness.
questions.trap: An outbox prevents a lost publication gap, but does not magically prevent every duplicate.
questions.exercise: The relay publishes and crashes before updating its outbox row. What should the consumer do on redelivery?
questions.solution: Check or claim the event ID using a durable uniqueness rule in the consumer's transaction with its state change. A duplicate can acknowledge the already applied result. External side effects need their own idempotency key or reconciliation.
questions.followUp: How do you retain deduplication records long enough without unbounded storage growth?

questions.title: Design a rate-limited job platform
questions.prompt: How would you design a multi-tenant Go job service at 100,000 jobs per minute?
answerPoints: Clarify job duration, payload size, ordering, maximum queue age, durability, tenant isolation and acceptable duplicate execution. Requests per minute alone do not determine CPU, storage or concurrency requirements.

Bound admission per tenant and globally, persist accepted work before acknowledging according to the promised durability, and use leases with recovery. Workers must make side effects idempotent because lease expiry and crashes can permit re-execution.

Estimate active work using arrival rate × service time, then account for burst headroom and dependency limits. Track queue age, throughput, retry volume, saturation and outcome, and rehearse overload and worker loss. Prefer the simplest topology that meets those measured constraints.
questions.trap: A Redis lock or a large worker count is not a complete scheduling, durability or fairness design.
questions.exercise: Jobs take two seconds on average. Estimate average active jobs and explain why that is not the final worker count.
questions.solution: 100,000/60 is about1,667 jobs/second; at2 seconds, about3,334 jobs are active on average in a stable system. Tail durations, CPU/I/O mix, quotas, retries and headroom determine limits. If capacity is lower than intake, queue age grows without bound unless admission changes.
questions.followUp: What do you promise a client when its acceptance response is lost after the job was persisted?

questions.title: One request, one time budget
questions.prompt: Which timeouts should a production Go HTTP service configure?
answerPoints: Distinguish incoming server read/header/write/idle controls from outgoing client and transport timeouts. A client timeout and a request context constrain different scopes; use a shared Transport/Client instead of rebuilding pools for each call.

Propagate a request context to storage and outbound calls. Budget time across attempts, backoff and response work rather than allowing every downstream operation a full independent timeout. Request bodies and response reads need size limits.

Drain/close response bodies according to the API contract so reusable connections can be reclaimed. Treat cancellation and timeout as outcomes, and never assume a timed-out write did not reach its server.
questions.trap: A server WriteTimeout is not a universal cancellation mechanism for every goroutine doing application work.
questions.exercise: Your endpoint has a500 ms budget and calls two dependencies serially. How should retries fit?
questions.solution: Allocate less than the full500 ms to each stage and reserve response time. Retry only classified transient, safe operations while the remaining deadline permits. Measure the actual end-to-end latency, including pool checkout and backoff.
questions.followUp: How can a slow response body exhaust connections even if dialing is fast?

questions.title: Authorization and hostile input
questions.prompt: What must a Go API validate beyond successful JSON decoding?
answerPoints: Bound body bytes and decoding work, validate required values and reject unsupported fields if the API contract requires it. Validate identifiers and ranges; decoding into a struct does not establish business validity.

Authenticate identity and authorize every target resource, including tenant scope. Do not trust a tenant ID supplied by the client without binding it to the caller's rights. Parameterize database operations and avoid building shell commands from request strings.

Protect secrets in logs, errors and traces. Use TLS and deployment-level controls, and handle replay/idempotency on sensitive operations. Escaping output is specific to its context; HTML, SQL and a shell have different rules.
questions.trap: A valid JWT says who a request claims to be; it does not authorize every object ID in the URL.
questions.exercise: A user requests /orders/another-tenant-order. Where should the tenant predicate be enforced?
questions.solution: Include the authorized tenant scope in the authoritative lookup/update predicate and test cross-tenant access. A UI filter or a precheck followed by an unscoped write leaves a security gap.
questions.followUp: How would you test oversized JSON and an expensive but syntactically valid nested payload?

questions.title: Idempotent API operations
questions.prompt: How should POST /payments behave when the caller retries?
answerPoints: Accept a stable idempotency key with an explicit scope, retention policy and request fingerprint. Two requests using the same key for different payloads should conflict rather than silently share a result.

Claim the operation and record its outcome durably in the same consistency boundary as the state transition when possible. Concurrent requests need a uniqueness rule, not a check followed by an unprotected insert.

Return the prior outcome or an explicit in-progress state. When a remote provider owns the side effect, forward a stable provider key and reconcile unknown outcomes; a local transaction alone cannot roll back the remote payment.
questions.trap: An in-memory map of keys fails across restarts and multiple replicas.
questions.exercise: The provider charged successfully but your process crashed before persisting its response. What happens on retry?
questions.solution: Reuse the provider idempotency key or query its operation ID, reconcile the durable local record and return the known outcome. Avoid blindly charging again. Test this crash window with a controllable fake provider.
questions.followUp: How long must keys be retained if clients can retry after a day?

questions.title: Graceful shutdown and probes
questions.prompt: What is the correct shutdown order for a Go service?
answerPoints: Stop accepting new work and become unready, then allow a bounded drain of in-flight requests or jobs. Call Server.Shutdown with a deadline; force remaining cleanup only when that budget expires.
Keep databases, transports and result sinks alive until their users finish. Cancellation signals stop but does not join; explicitly wait for owned goroutines and stop periodic work.

Coordinate the process budget with the orchestrator's termination grace period and traffic propagation. Readiness controls traffic eligibility; liveness determines restart behavior. A failing shared dependency should not automatically trigger a restart storm.
questions.trap: Closing the database first makes otherwise healthy in-flight requests fail during deployment.
questions.exercise: A container receives SIGTERM with30 seconds of grace. Reserve a drain and cleanup budget.
questions.solution: Transition readiness immediately, initiate a bounded drain shorter than the full30 seconds, wait for owned workers, then close shared clients. Leave headroom for signal delivery and infrastructure lag; measure a rolling deployment under live traffic.
questions.followUp: What happens to hijacked connections or long-lived streams during Shutdown?

questions.title: SQL pools, transactions and N+1
questions.prompt: What does sql.DB own, and why can increasing its pool hurt?
answerPoints: sql.DB is a concurrency-safe pool handle, not one connection. Reuse it for the application lifetime and size active/idle connections against database capacity across all replicas.

Use a transaction handle consistently for operations that must share its transaction. Calling db.Query from inside transaction logic may use another connection and violate atomicity. Always commit or roll back and honor contexts.

Pool waits, slow queries, lock contention and N+1 query patterns can dominate latency. More connections may move the queue into an already saturated database. Query count and execution plans matter as much as goroutine count.
questions.trap: Beginning a transaction does not automatically attach unrelated db calls to it.
questions.exercise: Fifty replicas each permit100 connections but the database safely handles300. What do you change?
questions.solution: Start from a global connection budget, reduce per-replica active limits with headroom, measure checkout wait and query duration, and fix inefficient access patterns. Autoscaling replicas must not accidentally multiply database pressure without a corresponding budget.
questions.followUp: Why might a slow transaction cause a pool-exhaustion incident even without a connection leak?

questions.title: Streaming, backpressure and ordering
questions.prompt: How do you stream millions of records without retaining them all?
answerPoints: Read bounded batches and write incrementally, allowing the downstream rate to regulate production. Avoid collecting all results before encoding or launching an unbounded goroutine for each record.

Carry cancellation from client disconnects to cursors and producers, close iterators, check iteration and encoding errors, and bound output buffers. Decide whether ordering requires a bounded reorder buffer when work is parallel.
Once a response starts, ordinary HTTP status changes may be unavailable; define an in-stream error protocol or resume cursor. Resume tokens must have stable ordering and correct authorization scope.
questions.trap: Using a channel does not ensure bounded memory if the producer also accumulates a full slice.
questions.exercise: A client reads one record per second while the database produces1,000. Where does the queue live?
questions.solution: It must be a bounded buffer under your control, eventually slowing the database cursor or cancelling by deadline. Track buffer occupancy and time blocked on writes; never let hidden queues grow forever.
questions.followUp: How do you preserve order while one record takes ten times longer to transform?

questions.title: Tests that prove behavior
questions.prompt: What makes a good table-driven test?
answerPoints: Each case states an input, an observable expected result and the behavior it protects. Include boundaries and meaningful failure paths, not just a list of ordinary inputs.
Use subtest names to explain the scenario. Keep fixtures isolated and avoid mocks that merely repeat implementation calls; a fake at an external boundary should model realistic failures.

A passing test proves only its assertions on executed cases. Check errors, returned data and important side effects. Tests that accept either result or never assert a claimed invariant can pass while the bug remains.
questions.trap: Coverage counts executed code; it does not show whether the assertions would catch a wrong answer.
questions.exercise: For LowerBound, choose four cases that catch an off-by-one and a duplicate-boundary error.
questions.solution: Use empty input→0, target below all→0, target above all→n, and duplicate target→first equal index. Add a property that all elements before the answer are smaller and none at/after it are smaller.
questions.followUp: How would you show the test fails for the old buggy implementation?

questions.title: Parallel tests without shared state
questions.prompt: Why does a test pass alone but fail with t.Parallel?
answerPoints: Parallel cases can overlap access to global variables, files, environment, shared database rows and fake servers. A shared mutable fixture makes outcomes depend on scheduling.

Create independent fixtures and unique names/temporary directories, and register cleanup with the right lifetime. Do not use sleep to order tests. Process-wide environment changes are incompatible with uncontrolled parallel execution.
Distinguish a flaky assertion from an actual product race. Use the race detector on representative paths and synchronize test barriers so failures reproduce without timing guesses.
questions.trap: Capturing a loop variable is not the only cause of parallel-test bugs; modern loop semantics do not isolate fixtures.
questions.exercise: Two tests clear the same Redis database before running. How do you make them safely parallel?
questions.solution: Use dedicated test instances or unique namespaced keys with scoped cleanup and no global FLUSHDB. Ensure the test account cannot reach production. A unique prefix does not help if cleanup still deletes every key.
questions.followUp: What changes if a subtest owns a resource whose parent defers Close before children run?

questions.title: Fuzzing parsers with useful properties
questions.prompt: What property would you fuzz for a custom codec?
answerPoints: A round-trip property checks Decode(Encode(x)) against a canonical form of x; decoder-only fuzzing should also assert bounded handling and no unexpected panic for arbitrary bytes. Seed known boundary and regression cases.

Define invalid-input behavior and resource limits first. Fuzzing a decoder that allocates directly from untrusted lengths can exhaust resources before finding useful bugs. Do not compare representations whose order is intentionally unspecified.

Keep minimized failures as regression seeds. Fuzzing explores inputs, but cannot prove protocol security or cover every concurrency schedule; complement it with examples, limits and targeted race/fault tests.
questions.trap: “Does not panic” is weaker than correct parsing and does not detect silent corruption.
questions.exercise: An encoder sorts map keys before serialization. What should the round-trip comparison assert?
questions.solution: Assert semantic key/value equality after decode, not the original map iteration order. Separately test deterministic encoded bytes and reject length prefixes exceeding the configured bound.
questions.followUp: How would you fuzz a streaming decoder with arbitrary chunk boundaries?

questions.title: Benchmark versus load test
questions.prompt: Why can a faster microbenchmark still make production slower?
answerPoints: A microbenchmark isolates a chosen code path; production includes concurrency, queueing, network calls, larger inputs and allocations that interact with GC. Benchmark data must resemble the actual workload.
Report allocations and compare repeated runs under controlled conditions. Avoid dead-code elimination, including setup in the timed loop unintentionally, and changing several things at once.

A load test needs an arrival model, duration, warmup, resource budget and latency distribution including failures. A closed-loop client can hide overload by sending less when the server slows; inspect offered and achieved load.
questions.trap: Average latency and a single benchmark run conceal p99 regression and instability.
questions.exercise: Optimization improves ns/op but doubles retained buffers. What evidence decides whether to ship?
questions.solution: Compare allocation/live-heap profiles and request throughput/p99 at the same offered load and container budget. Include burst and sustained phases. A local speedup may be a service-level regression under memory pressure.
questions.followUp: Why should timeouts and rejected requests remain in the load-test report?

questions.title: CPU, heap, block and trace
questions.prompt: Which diagnostic would you collect first for a p99 incident?
answerPoints: Start from the symptom and resource signals. CPU saturation suggests a CPU profile; growing live memory suggests a heap profile; lock waits suggest mutex/block profiles; scheduling and cross-goroutine timing often need a runtime trace.

Different profiles answer different questions. Allocation-space shows churn while in-use space shows retention at capture time. A blocked network call may explain latency without appearing as a hot CPU stack.

Collect safely with limited overhead and protected access. Compare equivalent load windows and correlate with request/queue/dependency metrics. Do not expose profiling endpoints publicly or attach high-cardinality private request data to metrics.
questions.trap: The largest CPU function is not automatically the source of a latency tail caused by waiting.
questions.exercise: CPU is low, goroutine count rises and requests wait for DB connections. What do you inspect?
questions.solution: Inspect pool checkout metrics, goroutine stacks, slow/long transactions and connection ownership. More CPU profiling alone is unlikely to resolve a dependency wait. Bound intake while recovering the underlying capacity.
questions.followUp: What evidence distinguishes a deadlock from a healthy service that is simply overloaded?

questions.title: Fault tests around unknown outcomes
questions.prompt: How do you test a retry protocol instead of just a retry loop?
answerPoints: Enumerate failure boundaries: before send, after remote commit, before reply, after local persistence and during shutdown. The same timeout error can correspond to different durable outcomes.

Use a controllable dependency to pause at each boundary, crash/restart the caller and replay the same operation ID. Assert the business invariant, such as one charge, not a specific number of network calls.

Test concurrent duplicates, exhausted budgets and retention expiry. Separate local deterministic tests from integration tests that verify the actual store's atomicity and durability settings. Record what a mock cannot prove.
questions.trap: A fake that always fails before committing cannot validate idempotency after an ambiguous timeout.
questions.exercise: Write the invariant for a consumer that may receive an event twice after restart.
questions.solution: For every durable event ID, its business state transition is applied at most once within the chosen authoritative store, while already applied events can be acknowledged again. A transaction/unique constraint must make the claim and mutation atomic.
questions.followUp: Which failure modes would still exist if the side effect is an external email or payment?

questions.title: Package, module and repository
questions.prompt: Why can a repository contain several packages but only one module path in one go.mod?
answerPoints: A package groups Go files compiled together in a directory, subject to build constraints. A module is a versioned set of packages rooted at go.mod; a repository is a version-control container and can hold multiple modules.
Import paths combine module path and package subdirectory. A nested go.mod creates a new module boundary; changes inside it may require its own tests and release version. Import cycles are rejected.

A v2+ module normally includes the major version suffix in its module/import path. internal packages enforce an import visibility boundary. A folder layout or repository rename can therefore change public API identity.
questions.trap: A Git branch name or checkout directory is not the module import path.
questions.exercise: A repository root is example.com/acme and contains cmd/api and internal/store. Which is the executable package?
questions.solution: cmd/api normally has package main and builds an executable; internal/store is an importable package restricted to the permitted parent tree. The module path still comes from go.mod. Verify with go list ./... instead of guessing from filenames.
questions.followUp: What changes if internal/store gains its own go.mod?

questions.title: Version selection and checksums
questions.prompt: Why did changing one dependency upgrade another?
answerPoints: Minimal version selection chooses the highest required minimum version of each module in the build list. Adding a dependency can raise a transitive minimum even if your direct requirement did not change.

go.sum authenticates module content hashes; it does not select versions or act as a lockfile. The proxy and checksum database have separate roles, and private module configuration changes where requests are sent.

Inspect go mod graph, go list -m all and go mod why before changing pins. A replace directive changes source selection in the main module/workspace and can mask a compatibility failure that consumers will still see.
questions.trap: Forcing an older indirect version cannot satisfy a newer minimum without changing the graph or source.
questions.exercise: A requires C1.2; B requires C1.5. Which C is selected, and what would go.sum decide?
questions.solution: C1.5 is selected by the graph. go.sum verifies the selected module's bytes; it does not choose C1.2 or pin the graph to the first downloaded version. Test the actual selected module list in CI.
questions.followUp: How does a major-version suffix allow v1 and v2 APIs to coexist?

questions.title: go.work, replace and release consumers
questions.prompt: Why can code work in a workspace but fail for users?
answerPoints: A workspace can use local module checkouts together. A local replace can redirect dependencies to edited source that has never been released. These are development conveniences, not a published dependency guarantee.

An independently consumed module must build from its own go.mod with released dependencies. Test it with workspace influence disabled and a clean module cache when investigating hidden local assumptions.
Keep generated files, embedded assets and platform build constraints in the test matrix. A developer workstation may have an untracked generated file or a native tool that CI lacks.
questions.trap: Committing go.work does not release every module's unpublished API to downstream consumers.
questions.exercise: Your library imports a new function from a local sibling module. What must happen before release?
questions.solution: Release the sibling API under a valid version, require that version and test the library independently using GOWORK=off. If compatibility requires it, update the library's public contract and version too.
questions.followUp: How would CI detect a stale generated file or missing go:embed asset?
questions.code:
GOWORK=off go test ./...
go list -m all

questions.title: Private dependencies and supply chain
questions.prompt: How do you keep private module names and credentials out of public services?
answerPoints: Configure the private module patterns and appropriate proxy/checksum behavior before fetching. GOPRIVATE is a policy input for module handling; it is not a credential store or access grant.
Use scoped credentials via the supported transport, never embed tokens in module paths, committed URLs or Docker layers. Keep CI secrets out of logs and untrusted build steps.

Review module graph changes, hashes and supported toolchain versions. Pin build inputs and scan reachable vulnerabilities with current tooling, but distinguish an advisory match from an exploitable path and do not promise that a scan proves safety.
questions.trap: Turning off checksum verification globally to fix one private dependency weakens verification for public dependencies too.
questions.exercise: A CI build prints a Git URL containing a token. What is the immediate and durable repair?
questions.solution: Revoke/rotate the exposed credential, restrict log access as appropriate, then move authentication to a secret mechanism that does not appear in source or command output. Review the build path before rerunning; do not paste the token into an agent prompt.
questions.followUp: How can an unreviewed dependency or build script read credentials present in its environment?

questions.title: Build reproducibility and resource budgets
questions.prompt: Why does go test ./... fail only under a small CI container?
answerPoints: Compilation and test execution both consume memory, processes and CPU. Package build parallelism, test parallelism and each test's own worker count are separate multipliers.

Inspect the actual failure: OOM kill, timeout, missing native library, unavailable network or flaky shared fixture need different fixes. Caches improve speed but should not be required for correctness.

Pin toolchain and dependencies, validate platform/build tags, bound concurrency and retain useful logs. Reproducible source inputs do not automatically guarantee bit-identical binaries unless paths, flags, generated artifacts and other inputs are controlled.
questions.trap: Increasing the timeout cannot recover a process that the kernel killed for exceeding memory.
questions.exercise: A test suite runs8 packages ×8 paralleltests ×16 workers. How should you approach its load?
questions.solution: Treat the combined concurrency as a budget, not three independent defaults. Measure peak memory and dependency demand, then cap the appropriate layers and isolate heavy integration tests. Do not suppress failing cases to make the build green.
questions.followUp: Which evidence would you retain to distinguish a compile OOM from a test-process OOM?

questions.title: API evolution and toolchain changes
questions.prompt: How do you upgrade a Go service without silently changing its contract?
answerPoints: Review compiler/runtime release notes, module graph changes and API behavior separately. The go directive and toolchain selection affect the effective build environment; transitive dependencies may raise minimum requirements.
